analysis.one_liner: Requires large credit-card-issuing banks to let merchants route transactions over competing card networks instead of only Visa or Mastercard.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved: introduced January 13, 2026, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where no action has been taken since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to require the Federal Reserve to write rules barring large card issuers and networks from locking credit card processing to one or two dominant networks. Issuers with more than $100 billion in assets would have to enable competing networks on their cards, and merchants would gain the right to route transactions over those networks without penalties. Cards from networks that own their own issuer (such as American Express-style models) and networks flagged as national security risks would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants and small businesses that accept credit cards would gain the right to route transactions over cheaper competing networks, and if savings are passed through, consumers could see lower prices. Rival payment networks would gain access to transactions currently locked to the dominant networks.

how_it_helps.text: It would bar large issuers from restricting a credit card's processing to a single network or to the two largest networks by market share, forcing cards to enable smaller competing networks.
It would prohibit card issuers and networks from penalizing merchants for routing transactions to a qualifying network, or from locking in security technology that rival networks cannot use.
It would create a Federal Reserve-maintained public list of card networks deemed national security risks or owned by foreign state entities, which are excluded from routing options.

analysis.who_pays: Large card-issuing banks and the dominant card networks would lose interchange and processing revenue, and banks argue cardholders could lose rewards or face new fees if banks recoup that income.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue that weaker network competition requirements could reduce card security and rewards, because banks might offset lost swipe-fee revenue by raising card fees, cutting rewards programs, or tightening credit standards — costs that would fall on cardholders.

The bill imposes a one-size-fits-all routing mandate on issuers above $100 billion in assets; some community-bank and issuer concerns center on implementation costs and on the Federal Reserve picking which two networks qualify by market share, a determination that must be revisited every three years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — lower card-processing costs for merchants, with some chance of pass-through to prices — comes with real uncertainties: banks could raise fees or tighten credit to replace lost swipe-fee revenue, and the security of routing less-secure network alternatives through every large bank's cards would need to work in practice. The bill's fate so far is procedural, not substantive: it has simply not moved in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, vote, or further action since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 13, 2026 by Senator Marshall, joined by Senators Durbin and Welch, and immediately referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Its only actions to date are introduction, reading twice, and the committee referral; no markup, vote, or floor action has occurred.
It has five cosponsors split across both parties: two Senate Democrats, two Senate Republicans, and one Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the large banks that issue their cards are better off so far, since the bill has not advanced toward a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Visa, Mastercard, and large card-issuing banks

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors split across parties — two Senate Democrats, two Senate Republicans, and one Independent — with bipartisan sponsorship from Marshall, Durbin, and Welch at introduction.

industries.note: The bill would end their near-exclusive routing on large banks' credit cards by forcing merchants to be able to route over competing networks, directly threatening the interchange-driven fee income that flows through the two dominant networks.

industries.industry: Large banks issuing credit cards (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: Covered issuers would lose control over which networks process their cards, threatening interchange revenue that funds card rewards and other bank income.
Retailers pay the swipe fees on credit card transactions and would gain routing choice, which they argue leads to lower fees and, potentially, lower consumer prices.

industries.industry: Smaller and alternative payment card networks
industries.note: Networks other than the two dominant ones would gain access to routing on cards they are currently locked out of by issuer contracts.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since its January 2026 referral and only five cosponsors, the bill faces long odds: most bills referred to the Senate Banking Committee without a scheduled markup die quietly at the end of the Congress. Similar versions of this legislation failed to reach the floor in prior Congresses despite merchant-group support.
